_doc: Registry of the operator state roots a test or gate run may never mutate (#237).
Path templates expand ${REAL_HOME}/${REAL_TEMP}/${REAL_CACHE}/${REAL_LOCALAPPDATA},
which scripts/check-no-escape.py resolves from the OS (SHGetKnownFolderPath / pwd),
NOT from the environment -- a sandbox that redirects HOME/TEMP must not be able to
blind the gate that polices it. ${VAR} also expands from the environment.
mode=exclusive: the project owns this root outright and no third party writes it.
ANY added, removed, or modified entry is a leak and fails the build. Full recursive
sha256 manifest. No attribution needed -- every delta is ours by definition.
mode=signature: the operator and the OS also write here (%TEMP%, $HOME), so a strict
whole-root assertion would fail on unrelated third-party churn and get switched off.
A signature-matching delta is a leak ONLY when CAUSALLY attributable to this run's
launcher process tree (#278: a `cargo test` in the operator's own Calyx checkout drops
calyx-* dirs here too -- name matching alone false-positives). Attribution comes from
the launcher's Job-Object process-tree manifest; a delta not traceable to our tree is
counted as foreign churn, never used to pass or fail. This still catches #133/#236: a
vault dir our test leaks carries our PID (std::process::id() in the name) and is owned.
mode=attributed: shared-by-design AND worth a full byte manifest (the CBM store: this
machine runs several codebase-memory-mcp MCP servers that all write _config.db here by
design -- #278). Hashed like exclusive, but a delta is a leak only when attributable to
our process tree (PID-stamped name, or a launcher-recorded owned path). Foreign MCP
churn is counted, not policed; our own #246-class write is still RED.
The gate FAILS CLOSED (ASTRO_NO_ESCAPE_NO_ATTRIBUTION) if any signature/attributed root
is declared but no attribution manifest is supplied: it refuses to fall back to the
unsound name-pattern classification (#278).
attribution.skew_margin_secs (invariant-4 knob): tolerance for the run-window and
pid-first-seen timestamp guards (#278 attempt 6). Sources it must bound: NTFS lazily
syncs the directory-entry duplicated file info that scandir/FindFirstFile reports, so
a cached dir mtime can lag a fresh-handle os.stat (attempt 6 measured 164-168 ms on
the two false-policed calyx-leapable-* dirs); FAT-class metadata granularity is 2 s
(the coarsest timestamp any policed filesystem would report); the Windows clock tick
is ~15.6 ms; Job-Object completion-port delivery of first-seen stamps adds single-ms
latency. 2 s covers the worst (FAT granularity) with the measured NTFS skew an order
of magnitude inside it. A pid-reuse false attribution would need a foreign entry
written INSIDE this margin of our pid instance's first-seen time -- vanishingly
narrower than the 20-minute window that produced attempt 6's collisions.

limits._max_hash_bytes_note: #280 (2026-07-13): raised 512MiB -> 2GiB after confirming legitimate operator growth, not a leak — the operator's own MCP server indexed C-code-leapablememory.db (320MB) into the real store between gate runs; the CBM-phase hermeticity manifest verified the store byte-identical across our runs. The limit bounds snapshot hashing cost only.
